source.title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective

accepted.question_text: Across heavy-ion collision energies ranging from sub-threshold beam energies through SPS, RHIC, and LHC energies, what is the full energy dependence of strangeness enhancement, especially for rare multi-strange strange and anti-strange hadrons such as Ξ and Ω, when the enhancement factor is defined by comparing strange-particle yields in nucleus-nucleus collisions with those in proton-proton collisions?

evidence.quote:
• What is the energy dependence of strangeness enhancement over the whole energy region, in par-
ticular for multi-strange (anti-)particles?
Usually, the enhancement factor E is deﬁned as:

accepted.question_text: Is there a distinct onset of strangeness enhancement between low-energy heavy-ion collisions, where sub-threshold phenomena dominate, and intermediate-energy collisions, where partonic degrees of freedom become increasingly effective, or is any onset washed out by additional hadronic medium effects?

evidence.quote:
It remains an open question if there is any evidence
for an onset of strangeness enhancement between low and intermediate energies. This should happen
in a region where sub-threshold phenomena (dashed line) do not play a role any more and the partonic
• Could there be an onset somewhere?

accepted.question_text: At intermediate heavy-ion collision energies, especially SPS energies and below, how much of the observed strangeness enhancement can be generated by hadronic-medium mechanisms such as multi-step hadronic reactions, resonances, or multi-meson fusion processes rather than by partonic matter?

evidence.quote:
that there is no discernible onset visible, due to additional hadronic medium eﬀects (dotted line) (e.g.
multi-step hadronic reactions, resonances, multi-meson fusion processes, etc.).

• To what extend can hadronic eﬀects cause a strangeness enhancement at intermediate energies (SPS
and below)?

accepted.question_text: Do current data and mechanisms actually explain the dramatic enhancement effects seen for rare strange particles at sub-threshold heavy-ion collision energies, including observations such as unexpectedly large Ξ−/(Λ + Σ0) and φ/K− ratios?

evidence.quote:
The Ξ−/(Λ + Σ0)-ratio is found
to be much larger than the statistical model expectation and theφ/K−-ratio rises dramatically towards
very low energies.
• Do we understand the dramatic eﬀects at sub-threshold energies?

accepted.question_text: Can the experimentally observed enhancement of strange-particle production in heavy-ion collisions be tied directly and convincingly to the formation of a quark-gluon plasma, rather than to competing hadronic explanations?

evidence.quote:
• Or, in other words, can ﬁnally a direct connection between strangeness enhancement and QGP
formation be established?

accepted.question_text: Does the charged-particle multiplicity density dNch/dη act as a universal scaling variable for system-size dependence of strange-particle production when comparing proton-proton, proton-nucleus, and nucleus-nucleus collisions across different collision energies?

evidence.quote:
it would be interesting to establish whether d Nch/dη does provide an universal scaling variable for all
energies.
• Does dNch/dη provide an universal scaling for system size dependencies (pp→ pA→ AA)?

accepted.question_text: When strange-to-pion yield ratios change with event multiplicity, is the relation between dNch/dη and the effective reaction volume V0 sufficient to explain the trend, or do additional observables beyond multiplicity and volume control the system-size dependence of strangeness production?

evidence.quote:
In the statistical model approach strangeness enhancement is described by the transition from a
canonical to a grand-canonical ensemble, which depends on the volume V0 of the system.
• Is the relation of dNch/dη to the reaction volume the only relevant factor (look at other observables)?

accepted.question_text: At all collision energies, does the observed multiplicity dependence of strange-particle yield ratios really follow the statistical-model transition from a canonical ensemble to a grand-canonical ensemble, including the expected strangeness hierarchy in which volume dependence grows with increasing strangeness content?

evidence.quote:
In the statistical model approach strangeness enhancement is described by the transition from a
canonical to a grand-canonical ensemble, which depends on the volume V0 of the system. In this pic-
ture a strangeness hierarchy is expected [16], i.e. the volume dependence gets stronger with increasing
strangeness content.

• Does the multiplicity dependence match the transition from a canonical to a grand-canonical en-
semble at all energies?

accepted.question_text: In very high multiplicity proton-proton collisions, do strange-particle-to-pion ratios saturate as the grand-canonical limit is approached, or do some species such as Ω/π continue to rise rather than leveling off?

evidence.quote:
If this interpretation holds, the particle ratios should saturate for pp collisions at very high multi-
plicities when the grand-canonical limit is reached.
• Is a saturation of particle ratios observed in very high multiplicity pp collisions?

accepted.question_text: Do we have a correct physical description of how strange hadrons are produced and propagate in low-energy heavy-ion collisions, where the relevant medium is hadronic and must be understood before drawing conclusions about any partonic phase?

evidence.quote:
These are
particularly important, since they are concerned with the behaviour of strange particles in a hadronic
medium, which need to be understood before any conclusions about the partonic phases of heavy-ion
collisions can be made.
• Do we understand the production and propagation of strangeness at low energies?

accepted.question_text: Is there experimental evidence that low-energy heavy-ion collisions exhibit sequential freeze-out of strange hadrons because kaon species have different cross sections with nucleons, so that K− and K+ decouple from the hadronic medium under different conditions?

evidence.quote:
Since the cross section of reactions with nucleons are
diﬀerent (σ(K−)> σ(K+)) due to strangeness exchange reactions of the K−, the rescattering with the
hadronic medium should cause diﬀerent freeze-out conditions for the two kaon species and thus can
explain the diﬀerent slope parameters [20].
• Is there any evidence for a sequential freeze-out due to diﬀerent cross sections?

accepted.question_text: At low collision energies, does the produced hadronic medium behave as a macroscopic system that can be described fully by a statistical model, or are there important low-energy strangeness phenomena that fall outside that description?

evidence.quote:
• Does the medium also at low energy behave macroscopically and can fully be described by the
statistical model?

accepted.question_text: Why does the φ meson, whose valence structure is s s̄ and whose net strangeness is therefore S = 0, nevertheless behave experimentally like a particle with nonzero effective strangeness, including its enhancement pattern and its unexpectedly broad rapidity distributions in heavy-ion collisions?
accepted.context_brief: Peculiar behavior of the φ meson

evidence.quote:
With its ss valence quark structure theφ-meson is eﬀectively a strangeness neutral particle (S = 0).
Nevertheless, it behaves in many ways as if it would have a non-zero strangeness.

Another so far unexplained
observation related to the φ is the energy dependence of the widths of its rapidity distributions
• Why does a non-strange particle behave so strange?

accepted.question_text: What is actually established about hyperon-hyperon interactions, especially ΛΛ interactions inferred from two-particle correlation measurements, given that different analyses of the same correlation data favor weakly repulsive versus weakly attractive interactions?

evidence.quote:
Using
the one by Lednický and Lyuboshitz [23], a weak repulsive interaction was inferred by the STAR
collaboration [22]. However, an alternative analysis [24] rather favours a weak attractive interaction.
• What do we really know about hyperon-hyperon interactions?

accepted.question_text: How much can improved knowledge of hyperon interactions and hypernuclear matter contribute to explaining the structure of large-mass neutron stars, particularly stars with masses above 2 solar masses?

evidence.quote:
The investigation of hyperon-interactions is a crucial ingredient for the theoretical description of neu-
tron stars. It may in particular be relevant for the understanding of high mass neutron stars with
M > 2 M⊙.
• What is the possible contribution to the understanding of large-mass neutron stars?

accepted.question_text: Why are yields of very weakly bound hypernuclei such as the hypertriton ³ΛH reproduced so well by statistical-model calculations, even though their tiny binding energies make their survival in a chemical freeze-out environment appear paradoxical, the so-called “snowball in hell” problem?

evidence.quote:
Generally, it is found that the
(anti-)hypertriton yields agree very well with statistical model expectations [26]. Since their binding
energy is very small, it is surprising that their yields are ﬁxed in a chemical freeze-out environment

• Why are the yields of very weakly bound objects (e.g.3
ΛH) so well described by the statistical model
(“snowball in hell”)?

accepted.question_text: Are hyperon properties modified inside nuclei or nuclear matter, as might be suggested by measurements indicating that the Λ lifetime extracted from hypertriton decay is slightly shorter than the lifetime of a free Λ?

evidence.quote:
Current measurements of theΛ-lifetime
from the decay of 3
ΛH seem to indicate that it is slightly lower than the one of a free Λ, which would
be an indication for a modiﬁcation of hyperon properties inside a nuclear medium.
• Are the properties of hyperons modiﬁed inside nuclei?
